# Draft:Shootings of children during the Gaza war

Background
Previous shootings of children
During the First Intifada, UNRWA reported treating 5,315 children for gunshot wounds in the Gaza Strip, of which 659 were injured due to rubber-coated metal bullets (often called "rubber bullets"). The GCMHP survey estimate 43,500 children aged 8-15 were shot by either live-fire or rubber-coated bullets during this period. A total of 215 children died as a result of Israeli soldiers' gunfire; in 20% of child gunshot fatalities, Israeli soldiers had prevented or delayed the children from receiving medical treatment after being shot. Some children were killed at anti-Israeli protests (which included stone-throwing), though 55% of the children killed were not confronting soldiers when killed. James Graff writes that the Israeli military likely had an policy of causing serious injuries to child targets, giving a number of reasons: the large number of children injured by gunfire, pattern of IDF soldiers using high-velocity bullets against children, and that IDF never disciplined its soldiers who prevented or delayed medical treatment for the children they had shot.
In a 2023 report, Human Rights Watch stated Israeli forces had shot 34 children that year.
Gaza war
As of 3 February 2026, a total of 21,289 children had been killed in the Gaza war, and another 44,500 were reported injured. Most of the child casualties were caused by the Israeli bombing of the Gaza Strip, but a significant number have been the victims of gunshot wounds, often a single bullet to the head or chest. In the year 2024, MSF conducted 93,254 wound care outpatient department consultations in the Gaza Strip: 30% of these consultations were for children under the age of 15, and 11.3% were gunshot injuries.
Shootings
In December 2023, a 3-year old male was shot at a fruit market in Gaza City. A video shows the 3-year old was still alive after being shot and lifts his head; he is then shot again and this time he's killed. The family witnessed their child being killed and the boy's father later said the shooting by the Israeli military was "deliberate direct targeting". The mother said the Israeli army "executed" the 3-year old child.
During the January 2025 ceasefire, an Israeli sniper shot a child to death in Rafah, and then Israeli soldiers opened fire on a man trying to retrieve the child's body; the incident was filmed by eyewitnesses.
In many cases, doctors were able to recover bullets from the bodies of children. Some of the bullets were .56mm rounds that are standard issue for all IDF infantry rifles, and also used by marksmen. From one 14-year old boy's abdomen doctors recovered a .50 calibre round usually fired from vehicle-mounted machine guns (but sometimes used by snipers too). Vehicle-mounted guns often have firearm sights for precision targeting, but they're not always used.
In January 2024, doctors working at Nasser hospital reported "targeted Israeli fire" against civilians, including children, as they entered or left the hospital. For example, 14-year-old girl was reportedly shot dead after she exited the hospital to get water, with doctors stating there was no active fighting in the area at the time and that she was killed by a single bullet. During the same month, an American doctor, who was from Chicago and volunteering at the Nasser hospital, treated 5 children (2 of them under age 10) he believes were shot by snipers. The American doctor noted the children were often shot with a “one large-calibre bullet” and the placing of the bullets suggested they were not hit randomly but targeted. Most of the children were shot in the thorax, the chest area.
In January 2024, the Barbakh was following Israeli military orders to evacuate an area west of Khan Younis. A 14-year old male, who was carrying a white flag was killed by an Israeli sniper, according to his family and witnesses; he was first shot in the leg, and then again in the head.
Sometimes children survived sniper shootings, but suffered limb amputations and spinal cord injuries that caused disabilities, according to doctors interviewed by The Guardian.
In December 2023, a 13-year old boy was killed on the 8th floor of a building as he played with other children. Witnesses described a quadcopter, fitted with a gun, shot the child through the window.
On January 21, 2024, Euro-Med Monitor reported that armed quadcopters killed 2 children sheltering at al-Aqsa University near Khan Younis. In February 2024, a drone killed a 16-year old boy and a disabled 17-year old male at a tent camp in Rafah.
On October 8, 2025, after the ceasefire, UNICEF reported four children shot by quadcopters.
GHF sites
In July 2025, CNN posted a video of a 13-year old boy killed by Israeli gunfire at a Gaza Humanitarian Foundation food distribution site. The IDF acknowledged opening fire on Palestinians but called it "warning shots", and said they don't deliberately target civilians. Médecins Sans Frontières reported treating 71 children (25 of them under 15) for gunshot wounds sustained at GHF sites. Both MSF and an American pediatrician who volunteered in Gaza said most of the victims of Israeli shootings at aid sites were boys and male teenagers, as those are the ones who would take the risk to bring food to their families.
British surgeon Nick Maynard stated that Israeli soldiers may have played a "game of target practice" of shooting civilians at GHF sites. Most of the victims were reported to be boys and young men, some as young as 11-years old. Maynard noticed a clustering of similar injuries on specific days that was far too obvious to be coincidental. Similarly, an American pediatrician volunteering in Gaza, reported:
Kill zones
In December 2025, two boys, aged 8 and 10, were killed while looking for firewood east of Khan Yunis. The IDF claimed responsibility for killing them, saying the children had crossed an invisible demarcation line and posed "an immediate threat" to its soldiers.
West Bank
In the three-weeks following the October 7 attacks, Israeli soldiers shot 37 children to death in the West Bank. According to B'Tselem, they were killed under IDF's "open-fire policy" that allows Israeli soldiers to ignore both IHL and their IDF's own regulations.
In January 2025, witnesses reported an Israeli soldier shot a 14-year old boy in Sebastia, Nablus and the soldier then "celebrated" as the child bled to death. One witness said the child was "hundreds of metres away" and posed no threat to the soldiers. The IDF said it would investigate, but declined to give further details, and residents of Sebastia said the investigation was a "sham" as previous such investigations don't result in punishment for the perpetrators.
In November 2025, Israeli soldiers shot a 14-year old boy at close range in the Al-Far’a refugee camp, then prevented ambulances from reaching the boy for 45 minutes while he bled to death. CCTV footage also showed soldiers apparently putting a stone next to the boy and then taking picture of the boy with the stone. B'Tselem said that shows IDF soldiers attempting to frame the boy for stone-throwing, and there have been cases of IDF planting evidence on Palestinians.
Methods of shooting
Palestinians in Gaza reported that hovering armed, remotely-controlled drones, resembling quadcopters, had been used to shoot at civilians during the war. These drones often also had a camera and a loudspeaker (the loudspeakers would often be used by the Israeli military to give instructions to Palestinians). Because these drones fired “single high-velocity” shots, they were also called sniper drones.
Evidence of deliberate targeting
The topic of shootings of children during the Gaza war was especially notable as many viewed this as evidence that the Israeli military deliberately targets children. Iain Overton said the evidence was "clinical, methodical, and damning". Doctors from Western countries who volunteered in Gaza say they saw evidence that Israeli snipers would deliberately target children. The PCHR said sniper fire that targets children,

International law
Reactions
Israeli military
Benjamin Netanyahu described the IDF during the war as “the most moral army in the world” and the IDF said it does not target civilians. But many Israelis, including Israeli soldiers, have said rules against targeting civilians are often not enforced. One former Israeli soldier said the army often "covers up" crimes by its soldiers; and not only do many soldiers don't report crimes committed by members of their unit, but they sometimes "celebrate" the killing of Arabs. For example, in 2004, an Israeli army captain that repeatedly shot a 13-year old girl to death was cleared of wrongdoing by an Israeli military court.
One Israeli sniper told The Guardian that most Israeli soldiers were careful but "there are those who regard all the Arabs as the enemy and find any reason to shoot or no reason at all".
